Although Anthropic wants to sell some of its shares to the public, its founders aren’t planning on losing control.

The company has devised a “Founder Voting Structure” which will give its seven co-founders majority voting control over the company, under a plan outlined last month .

Anthropic explains:

double quotation mark We believe that our seven co-founders, Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah, as a group, are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission. Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to a limited liability company of which our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members (the “Founder LLC”). Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors.

Anthropic's loss hit $80bn in first half of 2026

Anthropic’s IPO filing thrown a light on the company’s financial performance – where revenues and losses have both been growing at a remarkable rate.

The document filed with the SEC today shows that Antropic pulled in revenues of $16.2bn in the first half of this year, up from just $1.16bn a year earlier.

But losses surged to over $80bn in January-June this year, up from $12.9bn a year before.

That jump in losses was mainly due to a rise in the fair value of convertible notes, which can be converted into stock.

Anthropic warns:

double quotation mark We have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.

Anthropic files for stock market float

Newsflash: AI firm Anthropic has taken an important step towards floating on the New York Stock Exchange.

In the last few minutes, Anthropic filed publicly for an initial public offering, in which it declares that “AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history”.

If managed well, Anthropic says, it could rapidly speed up scientific discovery, “greatly increase economic growth rates”, help cure major disease and solve other serious problems.

But alongside the potential of AI, Anthropic – which operates the Claude chatbot – also points to the risks – warning that AI can be used “for ill as well as good”.

The word risks appears more than 200 times in the IPO filing – and those risks include the danger that AI is used for cybercrime or to design biological weapons, misused by authoritarian states, or that humans could lose control of it, Anthropic says.

It’s not immediately cleat what value Anthropic is aiming for – the section showing how many shares it will sell, and at what price, is blank….

Chinese online shopping giant Temu has agreed to take action to reduce the prospect of illegal goods being sold on its platform to comply with EU legislation.

It has now been given four months by the EU to prove it can remedy the breaches of the Digital Services Act.

Following a €200m fine in May, the website will launch a six month risk assessment of products along with an evaluation of the effectiveness of measures put in place to stop illegal products being sold on its platform.

The Chinese platform was warned it would face a series of rolling fines if it it did not do this.

Among the items the EU found on its website were baby dummies posing a choke hazard, clothing and jewellery with carcinogenic chemicals and electrical chargers failing basic safety tests.

SpaceX enters $4bn deal with Apollo for AI chips

Newsflash: We have another multi-billion dollar deal in the AI world.

SpaceX has reported that it has agreed to lease data centre hardware, including AI chips, from an entity managed by asset management firm Apollo Global Management .

The equipment will be leased for around five years, and used in data centres selected by SpaceX – which expects to pay roughly $40bn to Apollo under the deal.

The lease schedules are expected to commence during the first half of 2027 upon delivery of the GPUs, SpaceX says in an SEC filing.

Reminder: Elon Musk posted last night that SpaceX had “closed $40B of debt for GPUs”…

Oxford Street finally pedestrianised

On a wetter Monday morning than London’s mayor may have dreamed of, pedestrians walked freely through the temporary bollards onto a green welcome banner rolled along the tarmac, declaring Oxford Street traffic-free.

Sadiq Khan said it was a “momentous day”, with almost a kilometre of the capital’s most famous shopping street now pedestrianised, banishing the buses, bikes, taxis, e-scooters and pedicabs along with the private car.

After decades of discussion, the closure to traffic has come into effect in time for the busy Christmas shopping period, although the bigger transformation of the street, a £150m project including trees, seating and level “plazas” for events, will start taking shape from spring 2027.

Speaking on Monday morning in the John Lewis department store, Khan said he was proud to be “finally unlocking a new era”, noting that the first action plans to pedestrianise the street started in 1971 “when I was literally in nappies”.

The mayor, whose first jobs were in retail in stores in the street, said:

double quotation mark “This is a momentous day for Oxford Street and the capital. We want high quality shops that will atrract people here but also culture, hospitality, leisure, and people going to and from the office having a good experience and I’m confident we’ll get that.”

He added:

double quotation mark “We’ve seen over the last couple of decades this street in decline… Pedestrianising the street with great public transport links, more greenery, more seating, will link to a better experience all round.”

The permanent plans will depend on feedback in the first phase and testing, and Khan said London “would be closely monitoring these changes to make sure they are working for everyone”.

He added: “I want this to be a proof of concept – that investing in people rather than traffic leads to better footfall and spend.”

About half of the 1.2 mile street is now vehicle-free, roughly from Oxford Circus station to close to Marble Arch.

Many of London’s double-decker buses have traditionally run the length of the street and will now be diverted into neighbouring roads.

Claire Mann , chief operating officer at Transport for London , said there would still be “plenty of capacity for passengers” and it should not affect reliability. She said:

double quotation mark “People have said for some time it’s an unpleasanat environment to walk along, narrow and busy – the main movement through Oxford Street is pedestrians so this is us enabling people to make that journey in a nicer way. We’ll be monitoring to see if it does have an impact on ridership – but Bond Street and the Elizabeth Line does give you a way to arrive in style.”

The CBI reports that UK retail sales volumes contracted in the year to October at the slowest rate since April 2025.

VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs

Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia , in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.

The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran , as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.

Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.

Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.

It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.

Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.

The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories . It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.

Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”

Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.

However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions .

stories.body:
Experts say Bank of England unlikely to increase rates by full percentage point – and could lower them by end of 2027

Financial markets are wrong to predict the Bank of England will raise UK interest rates by a full percentage point or more by next summer, City economists believe.

According to market-implied interest rate expectations, the Bank is likely to raise interest rates at least four times over the next year, lifting the bank rate from 3.75% today to 4.75% by the end of July, and possibly to 5% – meaning five rises – by December 2027.

But a number of City experts believe such a sharp tightening cycle is unlikely, given there is little sign that the rise in energy costs is pushing up other prices sharply.

“If you look at the swaps market, and you look at what’s priced in for the Bank of England, you’ve got four rate hikes and then no cuts ever. And I think you’d be hard-pressed to find anybody that really agrees with that,” said James Smith, a developed markets economist at the Dutch bank ING.

“By next spring, I think they [the Bank] could be sounding the all clear, and by the end of next year they could be cutting rates again,” Smith told a briefing in the City last week.

Market-implied interest rates are calculated from the prices of a range of financial instruments, including derivatives such as “swaps”, to establish where traders think interest rates will be in future.

Economists cite several reasons why market-implied interest rates expectations are high. One is that these expectations have been closely correlated with oil prices since the Iran war began.

The higher oil prices have risen, the more rate increases have been priced in. An investor could be right that interest rates won’t rise as far as markets think, but if oil prices keep increasing in the meantime, they would face mark-to-market losses and potentially margin calls.

“It can get pretty painful, so a lot of traders are quite reluctant to take this risk until there’s greater certainty about energy supply and the extent of inflation this winter,” said Smith.

Many traders got burnt at the start of the current Middle East crisis, when most were positioned for further rate cuts this year, he said.

Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, also doubts that the Bank will raise rates as fast as the market pricing suggests.

“I do not believe that any mainstream forecaster thinks the Bank of England will hike to 5% by the end of next year with the information set we have today,” Raja said. “It’s not to say it won’t happen. But based on current projections, it seems less likely.”

He has calculated that a lot of the forecast interest rate rises is actually “baked-in risk premia” – where investors require an extra return to protect them from uncertainty or instability.

“Once we strip that out, we have estimated that there is only really ~50bps [half a percentage point] of hikes pencilled in,” he said.

after newsletter promotion

Deutsche Bank’s base case is for the Bank of England to take the bank rate to 4.25% by next February and then hold rates there until the end of 2027.

The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates to 4% at its next meeting, on 5 November, after UK inflation rose further above its target in September to 3.5% .

Last month Goldman Sachs said its probability-weighted forecast path for the bank rate remained “notably below market pricing”, although it does expect the Bank to raise rates to 4% next month.

Morgan Stanley’s base case is for rises in November and February, with rates on hold thereafter. But in a new research note, it suggests there could be additional pressure to raise interest rates if the Low Pay Commission recommends a larger increase in the national living wage than expected.

Oxford Economics , a consultancy, also thinks the UK rate-raising cycle will be much less pronounced than what is currently priced into financial markets.

“We forecast the [Bank’s] monetary policy committee will raise interest rates by 25bps [a quarter of a percentage point] at its November and February meetings, taking the bank rate to 4.25%. This is significantly below the peak in money market expectations, which currently point to the bank rate peaking between 4.75% and 5%,” they told clients last week.

Even Huw Pill, the Bank’s hawkish chief economist, has suggested market expectations are running too hot. He told an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok this month he was sceptical that the Bank would need to raise interest rates four times over the next year.

stories.body:
A person with depression might sleep much longer than usual and still wake feeling exhausted. Later that evening, when they want to go to bed, they may find themselves wide awake. Researchers are investigating whether patterns like these could help explain why antidepressants work better for some people than others.

The clue may lie in the body’s internal clock , which helps regulate when someone sleeps, wakes and feels alert.

An Australian study examined 11,380 people, predominantly with severe or recurring depression. About 23% met the researchers’ criteria for a proposed subtype called “circadian depression”, named after the body’s roughly 24-hour internal clock.

Participants needed at least three of six features, including being a night owl, sleeping longer during depression, morning tiredness and seasonal changes in mood or behaviour. The other features involved habitually sleeping and waking later, and having different sleep schedules on working days and days off.

Compared with other participants, this group reported less benefit and more side-effects from two common types of antidepressants, SSRIs and SNRIs, which affect how brain cells communicate through chemical messengers. However, some people with these sleep patterns still reported benefiting from these medicines.

The researchers also found genetic associations with later sleep timing, reduced sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar, and a protein involved in inflammation, the immune system’s response to injury or infection. These associations reflect inherited tendencies, rather than evidence that participants actually had blood-sugar problems or inflammation.

The findings are preliminary . Participants recalled their symptoms and medication experiences, and those in the proposed group generally had more severe depression. The researchers did not measure their internal clocks or establish cause and effect.

Some features overlap with recognised forms of depression , so it remains unclear whether this is a distinct subtype. All participants had European genetic ancestry, limiting how widely the findings can be applied. The 23% figure therefore cannot be assumed to represent everyone with depression.

How the body clock affects mood

The body clock coordinates roughly 24-hour cycles , known as circadian rhythms, which affect sleepiness, body temperature and hormones, the chemical messengers that help regulate the body. Light reaching the eyes helps keep this clock aligned with day and night. Meals and physical activity also provide timing cues.

When internal timing clashes with daily demands , sleep can suffer. Someone whose clock runs late may feel alert at midnight but have to get up for work while their body is still expecting sleep. Being a night owl is not necessarily a problem. Persistent disruption is the concern.

Sleep and mental health can reinforce one another . Disrupted sleep may worsen depression, while depression and stress can disturb sleep and daily routines.

One possible link involves brain systems that regulate emotion and reward , including the ability to enjoy pleasurable experiences. Animal experiments suggest that disrupting the body clock can affect these systems and produce depression-like behaviour.

In small laboratory experiments , researchers altered the sleep schedules of shift workers and people who did not work shifts. When their sleep and waking times were out of step with their internal clocks, participants reported worse mood. They had not been recruited because they had depression, and temporary low mood is different from clinical depression.

Conventional antidepressants might leave a timing problem untreated, but that remains a hypothesis. The Australian study did not test body-clock treatments, and its findings cannot establish whether someone with disrupted rhythms would benefit more from an alternative medication.

Could light therapy help?

Light therapy involves sitting near a specially designed bright-light box at a scheduled time, often in the morning. Morning light can shift a late-running body clock earlier , helping someone feel sleepy and wake earlier.

Read more: Why morning blue light therapy could improve sleep and daily activity in older adults

The treatment is used for seasonal affective disorder, depression that follows a seasonal pattern, often during darker months. Evidence suggests it can also help with depression that has no seasonal pattern.

A review of 11 clinical trials involving 858 people examined bright-light therapy for non-seasonal depression, including bipolar depression. Bipolar disorder involves depression alongside episodes of unusually elevated or irritable mood and increased energy.

In trials reporting remission, about 41% of people receiving bright light improved enough to fall below the threshold for depression, compared with 24% receiving dim light or treatment without bright light.

But these trials did not select people with the proposed circadian subtype, so they cannot tell us whether that group benefits more. Light may also influence mood through brain pathways separate from the body clock .

Timing and medical guidance matter. Light can shift the clock earlier or later depending on when it is used. People with bipolar disorder need particular supervision because light therapy can sometimes trigger unusually elevated or irritable mood.

Regular waking times, daytime activity and meals may also support daily rhythms . Melatonin, a hormone that rises in the evening and signals biological night, can help shift a delayed clock when carefully timed. However, studies have not established melatonin supplements as an effective depression treatment.

Towards more personalised treatment

Could measuring someone’s internal clock help doctors choose treatments? Wrist-worn activity monitors can estimate sleep patterns, while saliva samples taken throughout an evening can show when melatonin starts rising, offering a more direct measure of internal timing.

Researchers need to establish whether the proposed group really has distinct biological rhythms, then test whether choosing treatment based on those measurements helps people recover sooner.

For now, sleep patterns cannot reliably predict which antidepressant will work best, and the findings provide no reason to change prescribed medication without medical advice.

If future trials confirm a benefit, a prescription for depression might one day specify when to receive light as carefully as which medicine to take.

stories.body:
As Israelis head to the polls on October 27 one major issue that has not received serious attention during the campaign is Israel’s flat rejection of Palestinian statehood.

This puts Israel seriously at odds with world opinion. As it stands, 159 countries around the world recognise Palestinian statehood , including diplomatic heavyweights such as the UK and France . The two UN security council members joined Australia, Andorra, Canada, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Portugal and San Marino in formally recognising the state of Palestine in September 2025.

This represents an important shift within the world’s most important diplomatic frameworks. Now, nearly half of the G7 and four of the five permanent members of the UN security council – China, France, Russia and the UK – recognise Palestine as a legitimate state.

This international pressure was recently ramped up by international sanctions by the UK and others against Israeli settler groups. Given this pressure – as well as the ongoing conflict in Gaza – you’d expect opposition parties, at least, to engage with the record of the Netanyahu government on the Palestinian question. But there is silence. Not only from the government, but also from the opposition parties hoping to replace it.

The political parties comprising the ultra-nationalist government of the incumbent Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, champion “destroying Hamas”. They continue to flatly reject the notion of Palestinian statehood – to the contrary, they enthusiastically promote the expansion of Israeli settlements .

Netanyahu’s extreme-right partners, who he has depended on to keep him in power, include the Religious Zionism party of finance minister Belazel Smotrich, and national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power. These two parties want to go further. Their election campaign advocates the occupation of the whole of the West Bank. They back this with a euphemistically branded plan for “voluntary Palestinian emigration”.

The key contenders to replace Netanyahu are Gadi Eisenkot , the leader of Yashar (Straight), and Naftali Bennet , the leader of B'Yachad (Together). They have diverged from the Netanyahu government’s policy by promising to bring order to the West Bank by curbing settler violence. They both reject the idea of expanding settlements and promoting Palestinian emigration.

Eisenkot, widely seen as the most likely candidate to beat Netanyahu, says he is in favour of settlements that comply with Israeli law . He has also been a harsh critic of the massive E1 settlement. This is the massive proposed project which would – if completed – effectively cut the West Bank in half and make a Palestinian state all but impossible. Both Eisenkot and Bennet share the Netanyahu government’s stance of flatly rejecting Palestinian statehood.

Economy and security

The fact that Israeli political leadership is so out of step with world opinion on Palestinian statehood raises some pressing questions.

It was in September that the UK and 11 other countries announced a package of sanctions in response to settler violence and the signing off by Netanyahu’s government of the E1 plan. The sanctions directly target produce, goods and services from or associated with illegal settlements.

There has been discussion within the European Union of a broader package of sanctions , which could include stripping Israel of its preferred trading-nation status. In response, Netanyahu suggested that Israel might respond by using cryptocurrencies and blockchain technologies to evade such restrictions. This drew a stern rebuke from Israel’s central bank, which said: “The right course of action for the Israeli economy is to preserve economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy”.

Another big concern arising from the growing turmoil on the West Bank and the ongoing conflict in Gaza is the pressure this is putting on the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF). The IDF chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, recently issued a stark warning that the military already faces a manpower crisis. “I am raising ten red flags before the IDF collapses into itself,” Zamir reportedly told a security cabinet meeting. As well as its deployment in Gaza and across the West Bank and on Israel’s borders, the IDF also has troops in southern and southwestern Syria and southern Lebanon.

Despite the high stakes, the main parties contesting the Israeli elections appear to have no answers to these pressing questions.

Palestinian statehood is not an election winner

Opinion polls suggest the apparent lack of interest in a long-term solution for Palestinian self-determination may be a calculated strategy. There has been a significant shift in voter sentiment in Israel since Hamas’ October 7 deadly attacks. Many voters – particularly younger Israelis – are taking a hardline view towards Palestinians and Palestinian statehood. More than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support the far-right parties of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, according to a poll for one of Israel’s most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.

The majority of people in Israel reject the idea of a two-state solution . Many also see the growing international criticism of Israel as hypocrisy and evidence of a rise in antisemitism around the world. The key issues at the ballot box remain security, cost of living and who is to blame for the October 7 attacks.

The latest polling , which combines surveys by three of Israel’s major TV networks, has a possible Eisenkot coalition marginally ahead with 54 seats to 50 for a likely Netanyhu-led coalition. The margin is about 16 seats, reflecting the number of people who declare themselves undecided.

Once the votes are counted and a ruling coalition is formed, it’ll be for the next Israeli leader and whoever they choose to form a coalition with to work out how to deal with the serious challenges posed by the country’s growing isolation. It’s clear enough that the Palestinian question is at the heart of that. But the election campaign has offered no clues about how a future government might deal with it.

stories.title: Cybersecurity CEO Indicted for Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims
stories.summary: The post Cybersecurity CEO Indicted for Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A webpage with the words: “The World’s Leading Experts in IT, Cloud Management, & Counter Cyber Terrorism. Under Attack? Watch This Video Immediately!” A video appears showing a man with short cropped hair wearing a suit and tie with the caption: John Pistole, Former Deputy Director, FBI.
stories.body:
A federal grand jury indicted MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi last month for allegedly defrauding clients of his ransomware data recovery business, which was the subject of a 2019 ProPublica investigation.

A Florida man who was the subject of a 2019 investigation by ProPublica was indicted last month on federal charges that he defrauded clients of his ransomware data recovery firm.

According to the Justice Department, the man, Zohar Pinhasi, told customers he could recover their encrypted files without having to pay hackers, when, in reality, he paid the ransom and charged victims a hefty fee on top.

The indictment mirrors the findings from ProPublica’s 2019 article “ The Trade Secret ,” which centered on Pinhasi and his scheme. The outlet found that the ransomware victims were being harmed twice: once by the hackers, who locked their targets’ files and demanded ransom, and a second time by MonsterCloud, Pinhasi’s Florida-based data recovery firm, which misled its clients about not paying ransoms.

Read More

“By falsely claiming to decrypt ransomware without paying off the ransomers, the defendant re-victimized his clients while extracting a hefty profit for himself,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in an Oct. 7 press release. “Our Office will vigorously prosecute ransomware attackers who prey on Americans from across the world and those who cynically profit from their criminal activity.”

When ProPublica published its story in 2019, ransomware was growing into one of the world’s most pervasive cyberthreats. Hackers locked the data of governments, schools and businesses, holding the decryption key for a ransom payment, which they usually demanded in bitcoin and other types of difficult-to-trace cryptocurrency.

ProPublica’s reporting focused on how U.S. industries, from data recovery firms like MonsterCloud to insurance giants that cover ransom payments, all fueled the extortion economy . Ransomware remains a widespread threat today, and the threat to national security has grown as hackers linked to hostile foreign governments are believed to use ransomware as a cover for espionage. The prevalence of AI tools is also making it easier for attackers to spread ransomware.

Pinhasi, who went by the alias Zack Green, told ProPublica in 2019 that MonsterCloud never promised clients that their data will be recovered by any particular method. “How we do it, it’s our problem,” he told ProPublica. “You will get your data back. Sit back, relax and enjoy the ride.” He called MonsterCloud’s data recovery methods a “trade secret.”

Pinhasi hung up when reached on his cellphone this month. A message left with a representative at MonsterCloud’s office phone number and a message left with his attorney were not returned. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Pinhasi pleaded not guilty to the federal charges.

In its 2019 investigation, ProPublica interviewed MonsterCloud’s clients and ransomware experts and found that in certain cases the firm must have paid ransoms on behalf of clients. MonsterCloud’s services were particularly popular with local law enforcement agencies, who are loath to engage with or pay criminal hackers. Several interviewed by ProPublica at the time said they chose MonsterCloud to help them recover from ransomware because they believed the firm would never pay a ransom.

Pinhasi, who described himself to ProPublica as a former IT security intelligence officer for the Israeli military, said in 2019 that MonsterCloud handled up to 30 calls a day and had about 20 employees in South Florida as well as extensive global contacts.

Federal investigators found that, over the course of the scheme, Pinhasi allegedly charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million in ransom payments. In one example, Pinhasi made a ransom payment of about $8,200 but charged the client about $150,000. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in prison.

In the Justice Department’s October press release, an FBI official said Pinhasi had “turned the victim’s crisis into his own profit center. This deception is unacceptable, and the FBI is committed to ensuring accountability for those who choose to victimize the very people who trusted them for help.”

The Justice Department did not address ProPublica’s 2019 finding that one of the FBI’s own was among Pinhasi’s associates at MonsterCloud. John Pistole, a former deputy director of the FBI under Robert Mueller, was prominently featured in a promotional video on MonsterCloud’s homepage. “Police departments, government agencies, hospitals, small business and Fortune 500 firms trust MonsterCloud to help recover from attacks and protect against new ones,” Pistole said in the video. “MonsterCloud’s proprietary technology and expertise protects their professional reputations and organizational integrity.”

Pistole was not mentioned by name in the Pinhasi indictment.

In 2019, Pinhasi touted MonsterCloud’s ties to law enforcement as evidence of its integrity. Pistole, who also headed the Transportation Security Administration under President Barack Obama, was listed on MonsterCloud’s website as the only member of its “Cyber Security Advisory Council.”

Pistole did not respond to a request for comment for this story. In a 2019 interview, he said he became acquainted with Pinhasi after MonsterCloud reached him through a speaker’s bureau and that MonsterCloud paid him indirectly through that group. He said Pinhasi scripted his testimonial and that he was well aware that in most cases — including MonsterCloud’s — the only way to decrypt data locked by ransomware is to pay the hackers. “That’s the business model as I understood it,” Pistole told ProPublica at the time. “Based on my experience and knowledge, ransom is paid and they facilitate the best practices moving forward.”

A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on Pistole’s connection to MonsterCloud.

stories.title: A Texas Cop Signed on to Help ICE Deport His Neighbors. It Tore the Town Apart.
stories.summary: The post A Texas Cop Signed on to Help ICE Deport His Neighbors. It Tore the Town Apart. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A bearded man wearing a baseball cap and a dark uniform sits in a black Charger.
stories.body:
Co-published with The New York Times Magazine

Reporting Highlights

The Shadow Surge: In January 2025, President Donald Trump revived a troubled ICE program that deputizes cops as deportation officers. Over 29,000 local officers nationwide have enlisted.

After the Flood: Ingram, Texas, was rebuilding from a historic flood when its Police Department signed on with ICE. Within a year, cops would hand over the equivalent of 10% of the town.

Cop on the Ground: The local face of the national immigration crackdown became Officer Jaron Alexander. After suggesting ICE’s program to his chief, he grapples daily with the consequences.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

The new patrol officer parked his black Dodge Charger outside a house off Main Street and approached on foot. A Mexican ballad was playing. Someone had called in a noise complaint, claiming it sounded as if people were fighting.

But as the officer, Jaron Alexander, got closer, he found nothing of the sort. A middle-aged woman greeted him as her daughter, Joanna Martinez, petite and visibly pregnant, looked on. “What kind of party are you all having?” she remembers him asking. Behind her were three generations of an extended family. They were celebrating a 3-month-old’s baptism over pozole verde, horchata and beers.

Alexander ran some IDs and found no issues. The music wasn’t even that loud, he thought. He told them to have a good night, and then he left.

That encounter, in early October last year, was the first of many that Alexander and Martinez would have in tiny Ingram, Texas, a 1.5-square-mile town of 1,900 people beside the Guadalupe River. But it was the only one before Ingram signed an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that would roil the town and tear Martinez’s family apart.

“Her and I, at the beginning, I felt like we were running into each other all the time,” Alexander told us, in one of eight conversations over four months that offer a rare window into the thoughts of one of the local police officers on the front lines of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

In a town as small as Ingram, drivable in five minutes end to end, more run-ins were probably inevitable. Later that October, Alexander pulled over a work truck for rolling through a stop sign, and soon there Martinez was, demanding that he let her friends go rather than let immigration take them. He didn’t. He pulled over another driver in November who turned out to be her cousin, the father of the baby they celebrated at the baptism party. Alexander handed him over to immigration agents as well.

He pulled over Martinez herself a few weeks before she was due to give birth, she says, surprising her when he knew her name and the type of car she typically drove. He warned her that the car’s window tint was illegal and let her go. After that, he says, he caught a glimpse of her and her husband and their newborn daughter in the toy aisle at Walmart. Martinez told us she doesn’t think it was even her that day — her baby girl was then just days old, and she couldn’t imagine running errands with her so soon. But in Alexander’s memory, she was shopping for Christmas presents, just like him.

Alexander, who is in his mid-30s, with dirty blond hair already turning gray, says he didn’t come back to Ingram to help deport his neighbors. In his telling, he just ended up making it part of his job. The town was where he started his law-enforcement career years earlier, before he took a better-paying position with the county, as a sheriff’s deputy. But things recently started to fall apart, first in his marriage, next at the sheriff’s office: A 185-page internal investigation found that he had an affair before his divorce was final and used a county vehicle to carry it out, then lied about it all. He says the investigator called him an “embarrassment to the profession.” The sheriff’s office fired him. (Alexander said at the time, and again to us, that he did not have the affair.)

Ingram’s Police Department took him back just when its new chief — its eighth in five years — was under pressure from the City Council to do more: more traffic stops, more citations, more arrests, more numbers. Alexander says he told the chief that the sheriff’s office had a deal with ICE and that Ingram should look into it; maybe it could help the department grow. “Blame me,” he eventually told people. “It’s my fault in a way.”

Donald Trump had retaken the presidency with a promise to carry out “the largest deportation in the history of our country.” America was still figuring out what that meant. Finding and expelling up to 4% of the U.S. population — the 14 million residents who are estimated to be undocumented — wasn’t something a few thousand ICE agents could do on their own.

Underway in Chicago that fall, and soon in Minneapolis, was one version of how the administration could try to do it: masked agents from across the federal government surging into a liberal city to round up immigrants, beating back — even killing — the citizens who tried to stand in their path.

But a quieter kind of surge was spreading across the country at the same time. In September 2025, ICE announced new incentives for a partnership program known as 287(g). The program’s most aggressive form, the so-called task force model , which Ingram opted in to, enlists local police officers as deputy immigration agents, and the new incentives included a $100,000 vehicle stipend, a $7,500 equipment stipend for every participating officer, quarterly performance bonuses and funding to help cover officer salaries and overtime. “By joining forces with ICE,” the announcement read, “you’re not just gaining access to these unprecedented reimbursement opportunities — you’re becoming part of a national effort to ensure the safety of every American family.”

Alexander completed an online course with ICE a few weeks after the baptism party, qualifying him for time-and-a-half pay whenever he helped the agency pick up immigrants. Here in the Texas Hill Country, he soon became the local face of the national crackdown.

Ingram was just starting to recover from its worst natural disaster in a century, the flood that summer that killed at least 139 people up and down the Guadalupe River, including 25 girls at Camp Mystic. In the riverbed, towering bald cypress trees now stood at a lean, their branches swept back by a 30-foot surge of water and mud, their trunks still plastered with debris. As construction workers rebuilding the community traveled to their jobsites via Junction Highway, Ingram’s five-lane main thoroughfare, a black Charger began stopping them before they could get there.

Within three months of the baptism party, Alexander and Ingram’s other patrol officer had delivered at least 70 people to immigration agents, picking off what the police chief called a “dumbfounding” number of undocumented drivers. Within a year, they would hand over the equivalent of 10% of Ingram to ICE.

The weight of what Alexander was doing started to settle on him after Christmas. He says he was out patrolling as one of his new ICE handlers, a man in a ball cap and dark glasses, hovered nearby in an unmarked SUV. Around lunchtime, Alexander followed two Latino men in a 2008 GMC truck for several blocks before stopping them, they recall him saying, for failing to signal a turn.

A young man sat in the passenger seat. Alexander checked his papers along with the driver’s and determined that both were undocumented. The agent in the unmarked SUV rolled up behind them. Alexander realized who the man in the passenger seat was only after Martinez arrived in tears. It was her husband, Ulices Macias, the father of her newborn daughter.

“I don’t normally do this,” Martinez recalls Alexander telling her, “but I’m going to open up the car. I’m going to take the handcuffs off him.” He let the family have a moment together. In a video taken by Martinez’s younger sister, Alexander stood by, expressionless, as Martinez embraced Macias by the rear door of the Charger. He watched Macias cradle his 2-week-old baby girl, swaddled in a white blanket, and hug Martinez’s 4-year-old son, his stepson.

Then the ICE agent put the handcuffs back on Martinez’s husband, wrapped a chain around his waist and led him away. Alexander says Martinez threw herself to the ground and sobbed.

Images of the family he broke up shortly after Christmas would intrude on Alexander’s thoughts for months, he told us. But it didn’t keep him from doing his job. His next shift came a few days after he handed over Macias, and he was back in the Charger, back to stopping cars on Junction Highway.

“Mini Guanajuato”

Alexander says he didn’t always want to be a police officer. He describes himself as “kind of a chameleon.” He grew up in nearby Harper, tried a few different colleges without graduating and spent his 20s cycling though jobs in freight logistics, pest control and insurance.

Still seeking his calling, he arranged a ride-along with a police officer outside Austin. What sold him on policing was the suburban officer’s power to enforce the law as he saw fit. That day, they pulled over a woman who had a warrant out for her arrest. She was coming back from the store with children and groceries in the back seat.

“You can use your discretion,” Alexander recalls the officer telling him. Wouldn’t they be doing more harm if they took her? What would the kids do without their mother? And wouldn’t it all create more paperwork? The officer let her go. Alexander imagined himself making the same kinds of judgment calls. In 2021, he enrolled in the police academy.

Even before the floods, tensions were rising in Ingram. Hundreds of Mexican immigrants and their families had settled there in recent decades as an increasingly militarized border made it harder for seasonal ranch hands and other workers to cross back and forth. Latinos would come to make up 45% of its population, and some residents began affectionately calling Ingram “mini Guanajuato,” after the central Mexican state where many have roots. Yet when Alexander returned, Ingram’s City Council still consisted of six white men.

A council faction led by Claud Jordan, now the town’s mayor, and Rocky Hawkins, now the mayor pro tem, came to power in November 2020, in a revolt against a new sewer project. They abolished Ingram’s city administrator position and took direct control of the Police Department, cycling through chief after chief. Five former city employees say Hawkins regularly used racist slurs for Mexicans. Four say that he pressured the city to go after Latinos through code enforcement or targeted patrols, and two say that Jordan did, too. One of the employees recalls Hawkins complaining that Mexicans were “taking over Ingram.” (Hawkins and Jordan each declined to speak on the record or address detailed questions we sent them by email. In a brief text-message exchange, Hawkins said that none of it was right but declined to offer any specific concerns.)

These were the men the new chief, Dustin Breshears, had to answer to as ICE revived the task force program, which had been shut down for a dozen years until the day Trump returned to office in January 2025. ICE, under President Barack Obama, had phased out the program after some of the first sheriffs to participate in it, including Joe Arpaio of Maricopa County, Arizona, used it to disproportionately target Latinos in their communities. Investigations by the Department of Justice found that deputies in the task force program pulled over Latino drivers at up to nine times the rate of other drivers and that some retaliated violently against people who accused them of racial profiling. But now, under Trump, any law-enforcement agency, no matter how troubled or small, was encouraged to sign up.

Breshears began appearing at City Council meetings armed with statistics: number of arrests since the last meeting, number of traffic stops, number of cleared cases from the backlog of hundreds he inherited — and number of what he called “deportations.” (He later explained this was his imprecise shorthand for “immigration-related enforcement activities.”) At the council’s October 2025 meeting, held a couple of weeks after Alexander showed up at the Martinez family’s baptism party, Breshears reported a remarkable 162 traffic stops by Ingram’s two patrol officers — Alexander and Christian Perez, who was 25 — in just 20 days. (Perez declined to comment.) The officers made more stops in two months than the department had made in the entire previous year. The City Council gave Breshears an $18,000 raise.

Before Breshears arrived and Alexander returned in August 2025, the weekly blotter in The West Kerr Current, the local newspaper, documented the humdrum of community policing: loose dogs, neighborhood disputes, code violations. Then, suddenly, it was filled with drivers stopped for defective brake lights, damaged license plates, cracked windshields, illegal window tints or other unspecified “equipment violations.”

Breshears and Alexander strongly deny targeting Latinos. “It’s honestly not what’s happening,” Breshears says, noting that his half brother, wife and daughters have Mexican heritage. Ingram’s traffic stops were simply up across the board, he says, so more Latinos were getting stopped. He shared statistics showing that stops of Latinos were proportional to their share of the population.

Alexander, who on top of his roughly $70,000 base salary was now logging dozens of hours per month for ICE, told us the same. “I don’t care who’s in the car,” he says. “I really don’t.”

“El Charger Negro”

As the ICE program took hold in Ingram, warnings about Alexander and his black Charger — the department has several — spread through the Hill Country and far beyond. Groups on Facebook and WhatsApp seemed to track his every move. The Charger was outside Rita’s taco shop. The Charger was near Dollar General. The Charger was parked by the church. A member of one particularly active Facebook group texted him screenshots, and he scrolled through blurry photos of himself looming behind work trucks or leaning over car windows.

Many Latino motorists trying to reach worksites up the Guadalupe began driving an extra 90 minutes each day to avoid the section of Junction Highway that Alexander patrolled. Ranch hands began sleeping at their employers’ properties in nearby Hunt, coming to town only when they knew — or hoped — that Ingram’s officers would be off duty. Residents were rattled the day a Customs and Border Protection helicopter hovered above town and the elementary school went into lockdown as the police hunted for a Mexican man who had run from one of Alexander’s traffic stops.

One family notarized guardianship papers, in case the parents were detained and the children left behind. One woman swore Alexander showed up outside a memorial service and asked people for IDs. Another woman said he detained her and her husband when they returned home from church. Parties dwindled. Invite lists shrank. People began to move away, to Kerrville and San Antonio, and Alexander’s reputation reached as far as La Ceja, a village in the mountains of central Mexico, where an elderly resident said he and his neighbors were familiar with the Texas town’s police. “ El Charger negro ,” he said, with a knowing nod. He estimated that some 20 or 30 people in the village were recent deportees from Ingram.

Alexander’s fortunes seemed to rise as the Martinez family’s fell. With her husband gone, Joanna Martinez couldn’t afford payments on the trailer they shared. She and their infant and her 4-year-old son moved back into her childhood bedroom in her mother’s crowded home, where several relatives and their children also lived. She tried to stay connected with her husband, Macias, via WhatsApp calls while working as much as she could as a house cleaner to keep afloat. “I can’t lock myself up in my room and just cry,” Martinez says.

Winter for Martinez and her family brought a string of dark incidents. The January arrest of her cousin near the carwash as she drove to pick up her children from school. A canceled baby shower for her older sister, Jazmin, over a rumor that the Charger planned to show up. Another cousin, himself the father of a newborn, stopped and taken right in front of her mother’s house as Martinez watched.

A half dozen of the attendees from the October baptism party would soon be gone from Ingram, after being detained and deported or leaving to join relatives who had been. Some people had gotten wind that Alexander was making money off his enforcement. When a Spanish-language Facebook page shared a photo of him questioning the passenger of a beige Ford pickup, someone posted an animated image in the comments: a stack of green dollar bills growing taller and taller in an endless loop.

Alexander received his first ICE payments in early December. In January, as the country’s attention turned to the violent immigration crackdown in Minneapolis, he was often spending three or four hours a day and sometimes entire shifts working on behalf of the federal agency. By the time federal authorities announced a drawdown in Minneapolis on Feb. 12, Alexander had already made $3,264.46 from his task force hours, according to his pay stubs.

Ingram was by then one of more than 750 task force model partners around the country, up from not quite 500 when it signed up in October. At least 43 million U.S. residents , according to an analysis of ICE records by the legal data firm Titus Consulting, already lived in a county with an active task force agreement. Alexander was one of thousands of deputized officers in Texas alone.

In interviews, Alexander described the immigration system he was enforcing as “skewed” and “weird,” but he saw himself as largely separate from these concerns. “If you’re taking federal money to do a job,” he says, “I think you should do the job.”

Still, he seemed to struggle with the contradictions of his role. He told us he sometimes shared his lunch with the people he detained and that he let them hold on to their phones to call loved ones from the rear seat of the Charger. He handcuffed them with their hands in the front rather than the back so they could use their hands.

Martinez told us about a moment when she watched him detain one of her cousins. He allowed the man’s wife and children to hug him goodbye and waited until his 7-year-old daughter wasn’t looking to handcuff him. To Martinez, it seemed as if Alexander was trying to prove to her that he wasn’t a bad person. “But I’m not going to fall for it,” she says.

There was a protest in Ingram the following day against Trump’s mass deportations. Martinez decided to go. As she stood among a few dozen protesters waving a handmade sign with the name “J. Alexander” circled and crossed out, she saw him drive by again and again.

A few weeks later, Katie Winer, the leader of the group that staged the protest, was following the Charger after Alexander detained another immigrant in a traffic stop. He approached her car and threatened to arrest her if she followed him in the future, on charges of interfering with public duties. But he also seemed to want to talk, and she recorded him as they discussed what was going on in Ingram. “I think you guys are making a bigger deal of it than they are,” he said of the people he handed over to ICE. The only outliers were “loudmouths” like Martinez and “her little crew.”

Winer interjected that Martinez’s husband was the family’s breadwinner, and it was Alexander’s actions that tore them apart.

“My actions did not,” Alexander said. “His actions did. I made a traffic stop. He was here illegally. That’s not my fault.”

Still, Alexander’s uncertainty seemed to be growing. In March, another of Martinez’s cousins confronted him outside the taco shop, pressing him about Macias as she filmed with her phone.

“If I’m being 100% honest,” he said, “I don’t enjoy when families are separated, like with the Joanna situation. That kind of fucked me up.”

“I Voted to Get the Bad Guys Out”

A month later, as Ingram’s handoffs to ICE surpassed 100 people, another video of Alexander circulated among a small group of community members. It showed an evening traffic stop, at least the fifth stop Alexander made that day. He had followed a silver Ford F-250 from the highway until it pulled into the gravel driveway of a mobile home. There, the man in the passenger seat, a landscaper named Victor Ramirez Hernandez, tried to hurry inside. Alexander grabbed him before he could get there.

The truck’s driver pulled out his phone and began filming. “Why are you arresting him?” he asked.

“I’m not,” Alexander answered, struggling to place handcuffs on Ramirez as he squirmed. “I’m detaining him.” Then he wrapped his hands around the laborer’s chest, lifted him off the ground and slammed him down on the driveway. “I played nice with you, and now I’m done,” he said. He straddled Ramirez and cuffed his hands behind his back.

“He’s bleeding because you hit him,” the driver said evenly. They argued back and forth.

“You’re an idiot,” Alexander said, his face reddening. “Shut up. The more you talk it’s just making you look stupider.” (Alexander declined to comment on this incident. Breshears, who reviewed body-camera footage, says Alexander’s use of force was justified to control a potentially dangerous situation.)

Acrimony pulsed through Ingram that spring. In the Latino community, family members and neighbors accused one another of snitching, which Alexander says did happen. Young women accused one another of having affairs with him, which he denies, insisting that people just misinterpreted his attempts to be kind. “I’m friendly with the people that I meet,” he says, “especially when they’re friendly to me.”

One subject of these rumors was Martinez. She and her older sister scoffed at them. “He’s taken our whole family at this point,” Jazmin says. “And she’s going to sleep with him? It’s really annoying.” But some in the community, even cousins, stopped speaking with her. “It’s like ‘Hunger Games,’” Martinez says.

As Latinos fled and avoided Ingram, the daily takeout orders at one Mexican restaurant on the edge of town dropped to 50 from 200. A corner store catering to immigrants lost around half its revenue and most of its Latino regulars. Landlords in a mobile-home park just outside town struggled to find tenants.

But it wasn’t just Ingram’s Latino community that was reeling. For Ingram’s non-Hispanic business owners, including many Republicans in a county that voted 77% for Trump in the 2024 election, the immigration crackdown was becoming an outrage. It was taking people they worked with and knew well. It was interfering with flood reconstruction. It was hurting the local economy.

The owner of a heavily damaged strip mall on the western edge of town, Steve Edelstein, lamented the loss of two workers who were helping him rebuild. “Technically local law enforcement is doing their job,” he told a reporter for The West Kerr Current, emphasizing that he supported Trump. “But it isn’t helping the community.” A manager overseeing the rebuilding of Ingram’s Little League field, which was washed away in the flood, made an angry call to the city after two of his workers were picked up, Breshears says. A contractor helping rebuild Hunt’s destroyed post office had his crew reduced to eight workers from 30 — causing what should have been a four-day job to stretch to two weeks.

Among the people who called Jordan, the mayor, to complain was his onetime high school classmate Neal Secor, who describes himself as “one of the most conservative guys you’ll ever meet.” His family business, a cluster of rental cabins called Waltonia on the River, was nearly destroyed by the flood. He was struggling to rebuild. He says that in the spring, in two separate stops, the Ingram police detained four of his workers and handed them over to ICE — the second set as they returned from a job repairing the docks at a nearby youth camp, a favor Secor was trying to do for a neighbor.

Secor says Jordan’s defense was simple: You voted for this. They’d all voted for this.

“Let me tell you something,” Secor says he told Jordan. “I didn’t vote for this. I voted to get the bad guys out.” The two employees detained coming back from the youth camp were like family, his friends and co-workers for over a decade. “There’s still a lot of bad guys here,” he continued. “These guys aren’t them.”

Secor recalls Jordan saying that Ingram’s officers were just following the law. But, Secor wondered, why was it that he could drive 85 every day on the 75-mile-an-hour interstate and police officers just let him pass? He told Jordan he’d put 175,000 miles on his truck and never been pulled over. “It’s a matter of what laws you want to pick and choose,” he recalls telling the mayor. “We all break laws every day if you really want to get down to it.”

“God Wanted Me to Meet You”

On an unpaved side street in the Ingram hills in April, Alexander again faced a decision over whether to separate a young family. This time he had more of a choice; ICE had yet to arrive. A woman named Norma Luján took his hand and said she was praying for him.

Luján, 61, runs a successful housecleaning company based in Ingram. She had heard of Alexander long before she confronted him. She had seen him in the Charger, too: on the side of Junction Highway as she made her way to jobs at vacation homes or youth camps up in Hunt. On the side of the highway on the way back. In her rearview mirror for four excruciating minutes one afternoon as her “girls,” as she called her crew, held their breath and sank into their seats, protected by the tint of her car’s windows and the fact that a license-plate reader would show it was registered to her, a Texas-born U.S. citizen.

In January, at the carwash, Alexander had helped a sheriff’s deputy take one of Luján’s best employees into custody. The woman, Cinthya Carranza, was a single mother and asylum seeker from Guanajuato — and Joanna Martinez’s cousin. Carranza was on her way to get her children from school after she and Luján spent the day cleaning houses. Later that day, Luján saw a Facebook post showing a familiar face in a mug shot: Carranza’s. Luján broke into tears. To her, the arrest was a signal event. The Charger had mostly stopped men up to that point. This was the moment she understood that no one was safe.

Luján started losing workers in droves after Carranza was taken — some to traffic stops, most for fear of having to drive through Ingram. Her crew of 30 people dropped to fewer than 10. She worried for her business, but she worried more, she said, for her workers, the lives they had made in Ingram and the relationships she had built with them. They invited her to parties and baptisms, surprised her with presents on her birthday. She often led them in prayer. “I love them,” she says. She promised she would try to protect them.

When Luján’s employee Maria called that April afternoon to say the officer in the Charger was outside her house, detaining her husband as he returned from work, Luján jumped into action. Maria (who asked to be identified by her middle name because she is undocumented) was eight months pregnant and already terrified that she would have to give birth alone. Alexander had taken her brother a week earlier. Now Maria was hiding behind the curtains of her home, sneaking peeks outside, hoping Alexander would let her husband go.

“ Cálmate ” — calm down — Luján told herself as she approached the Charger. “ Cálmate. ” She took a deep breath. She says Alexander was sitting in the driver’s seat with the door propped open, staring at a tablet computer.

“Look, his wife has had a complicated pregnancy,” she told him. (This was true.) “She’s in the hospital.” (For that lie, Luján says, she later prayed for forgiveness.)

Then Luján reached out and grabbed Alexander’s hand. “I pray for your being, for your soul,” she recalls telling him as she cried. “I want you to think about what you’re doing. Feel it. Feel it, please.” She squeezed his hand. “I need you to look inside your heart,” she continued, “and let him go.”

Alexander didn’t react at first, in Luján’s telling. “God wanted me to meet you,” she said. He met her gaze.

“I’m that guy that everyone talks about on Facebook,” she recalls him finally saying. “If you think I don’t lose any sleep, you’re wrong.”

Luján pushed through the lump in her throat to speak. “I’m going to pray for you every night,” she promised him. She says Alexander squeezed her hand back, then pulled away. He walked off to make a call. She couldn’t make out much of what he said. It was quiet, save for the sound of Luján’s sobs and the pebbles from the unpaved road crunching beneath the officer’s feet.

Then he returned to the Charger. “Get him out of the car,” Luján recalls him saying. “Hurry up.”

“God bless you,” Luján said. “God will repay you for this.”

Alexander says he doesn’t remember the details of his interaction with Luján, but he confirms that he let Maria’s husband go, calling it a matter of “human decency.” He knew how hard it was to raise children. “A woman needs rest,” he says. “She needs help.” Maria’s husband “needs to be there helping out.”

At first, nothing seemed to change. Over the next two months, as the Hill Country prepared to welcome summer tourists and campers back after the devastation of the floods, Alexander worked around 100 task force hours, earning close to $5,000 from ICE.

But the next time he ran into Joanna Martinez, he seemed to be having misgivings. It was early June, and he was eight months into the ICE program. He had pulled over another of her family friends on Junction Highway, a person she had known since childhood. Martinez got a phone call and rushed to the scene, as she had so many times before. “I don’t feel good about this,” she recalls him saying when she arrived. “I signed up to be a cop, not an ICE agent.” (Alexander says he remembers that they talked and that he could have said something like that.)

Later that month, he pulled over a young man from Honduras who was on his way to a soccer game with his cousin, a 12-year-old with developmental disabilities. The boy’s father says he and his wife hid across the street watching it all happen, too terrified to step out and claim their son. The parents sent a friend from church, but she was not a legal guardian. Alexander says he had no choice but to hand the boy over to ICE, adding though that if he was one of the parents, he would see it differently. “If I’m in that position, there’s no way I’m letting my kid go,” he told us. “I’m probably fighting someone.”

Within a couple of weeks, Alexander’s task force hours dropped by about 40%, according to his pay stubs. It remains unclear if he tried to step back from immigration work or whether the number of undocumented drivers in Ingram had simply dwindled because of all he had already done.

According to Chief Breshears, Ingram had logged 194 “immigration-related incidents” as of this August. Whether every handover led to a deportation, Breshears couldn’t say. Alexander says he doesn’t know how many of the 194 are people he stopped. But he says he has now let at least 10 people go — many, though not all of them, mothers of young children.

Alexander sees this, and his relationship to the Martinez family, as evidence of his humanity, despite what people say about him. “For context, I’ve deported like six of their family members, and they’re still friendly to me,” he says. “So I’m not the monster they make me out to be.”

On July 16, the skies over Ingram opened again, dropping nearly 19 inches of rain in a single day, and the Guadalupe again overtopped its banks, again destroying businesses and homes. In the predawn darkness in the early hours of the emergency, Alexander began racing toward Ingram in his black Charger to help. He had barely left his house when surging floodwaters consumed the vehicle, destroying the Charger’s engine block. A driver in a pickup truck took him back home, and that’s where he stayed until the storm receded.

“One Free Pass”

Alexander remains only one cog in a deportation machine for which the federal government has now earmarked $240 billion. Today more than 1,900 agencies in at least 30 states have signed up for ICE’s task force model, with more than 29,000 deputized officers. With their help, ICE recently hit a record of immigration arrests, totaling more than 50,000 in August.

On Sept. 11, Alexander met one of us at a taco spot on Junction Highway. Ingram had changed in the year since his return. Whole neighborhoods had emptied out, and residents noticed fewer drivers on the streets. In part because of the money from ICE, the Police Department had hired two additional officers. As a Mexican ballad played over the speakers, Alexander warned against making too much of the leniency he showed to families like Maria’s. “It’s like one free pass, I guess,” he said: If he encountered her husband again during a traffic stop, he would probably hand him over to ICE. He just thought letting the father-to-be go was the right call at the time. “I mean, don’t you?” he asked.

He said he hadn’t made all that much money working with ICE. But city records show that his earnings from the agency already totaled $18,793.25 in nine months, more than a quarter of his base salary. “I think it’s skewed a little bit,” he said, looking at the pay stubs we had gathered.

Alexander said it was hard for him to be out in public anymore. He can’t escape being recognized in Ingram and Kerrville. Sometimes he catches Latinos staring at him, then walking away, visibly uncomfortable. So he tries to do his shopping and errands in another town 30 minutes away.

He blamed the Facebook groups. They had created a climate of “unreasonable fear” in Ingram. “What do they think I’m going to do right now?” he asked, seated at his table in the taco shop. A steady stream of customers, many of them white, approached a counter staffed by two young Mexican sisters. He said their father used to hide out in Hunt to avoid being pulled over in town. Some of their co-workers had quit months before, too uncomfortable to serve Alexander when he came in for breakfast. But when the taco shop owner sees him, he said, she hugs him.

“I know the status of everybody in this room,” he said. He suggested everyone who worked there was undocumented. Whether they disappeared or were allowed to stay was up to him. And today, at least, he was just there for breakfast.

“They’re fine, right?”

stories.title: President Apocalypse
stories.summary: While Trump campaigns for a Nobel Peace Prize, his war on humanity’s only home continues unabated. The post President Apocalypse appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .

stories.body:

Originally published in TomDispatch .

Do I even faintly believe the times I’m living in? The simple answer is: no.

Every now and then, I try to imagine going back in time to tell my long-dead parents about the world of President Donald Trump, which just happens to still be mine as well. Of course, they simply wouldn’t have believed it, not for a single second.

To put it in the context of their time on this planet, the only equivalent I can imagine would be if Sen. Joseph McCarthy, that anticommunist nightmare-and-a-half of the 1950s, hadn’t flamed out, been censured by the Senate, and died young but somehow had made it to the White House. But even he undoubtedly would have fallen short in terms of chaos and cruelty, if judged by the standards of Trump World. A President McCarthy might have been catastrophic for America, but Trump is on another level, an apocalyptic one.

Trump’s capacity for ushering in world-wrecking havoc is made possible by a character constructed almost entirely of flaws. His second term has been defined by global aggression and hostility. Yet he recently complained bitterly — and in a fashion it’s hard to imagine any other politician ever doing — because he wasn’t awarded a Nobel Peace Prize. As he put it , “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision.”

This is not only a petty man, but also a delusional one. As president, Trump has presided over more than 20 military interventions, armed conflicts, and outright wars who nonetheless swears that he “settled” eight conflicts and should have “ won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1 .” This includes a war between Egypt and Ethiopia that, of course, never happened and a failing war with Iran that drags on to this day.

If you’re going to “end” a war with bombs and missiles, then there are, of course, going to be casualties. A few thousand or more Iranians killed , obviously, and tens of thousands injured, not to mention ever-rising American casualties.

Frighteningly, the Iran war may not even be enough for him. He’s already starting to hint (if there even is such a thing as “hinting” in the all-too-blunt world of Donald Trump) that he might join Saudi Arabia in taking on the Houthi rebels in Yemen. “We’re going to look at it” was how he put it . I should really have added “again” there, since he essentially began his second term in office by attacking those same Houthis — killing large numbers of civilians in the process. But after the U.S. burned through $1 billion and failed to even achieve air superiority in Yemen, Trump ended the stalemate. Despite having vowed the Houthis would be “completely annihilated,” he announced a cessation of hostilities last May, leaving the group in control of most of Yemen’s populated areas.

Given American history — think the wars in Korea, Vietnam , Cambodia, Afghanistan, and Iraq, among other places — there’s nothing faintly strange about endless American military operations thousands and thousands of miles away from Washington, D.C., even for a president who said, upon taking office in 2025, that he would measure success by “the wars we never get into.”

A Grim Presidency

You would hardly know it from the mainstream press but one of those 20 Trumpian conflicts is the forever war in Somalia . And that war has an increasing domestic component. Recently, the Department of Homeland Security raided the home of Somali American Rep. Ilhan Omar in the Washington, D.C., area, aiming in some fashion or other to discover information that might help denaturalize her and so make it possible to eject her from this country.

As the president put it on Truth Social, Omar “left Somalia with NOTHING, and is now reportedly worth more than 44 Million Dollars.” Of course, who would know better about such things than the president of the United States who, in these years, is estimated to have made literally billions of dollars while in office ?

And yet, the never-ending war in Somalia, the nearby conflict we may reenter against the Houthis, and the failed war in Iran should be considered the lesser of the potential disasters that will sooner or later be associated with Trump. After all, he clearly has the urge to do nothing less than end this very world of ours , at least as we’ve known it, even if in a distinctly slow-motion fashion.

I’m not even thinking about nuclear weapons (although he admittedly still is ). No, I’m thinking about the president who, at the United Nations in 2025, called climate change “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world.” And since then, he has indeed done everything he could think of to ensure that this planet would get hotter yet. His Environmental Protection Agency, for instance, has recently repealed “rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.” And that’s just to start down a long list of what should truly be considered Donald Trump’s ultimate war on this planet of ours — including blocking wind power development and doing the same with solar power.

All of this is happening as global warming reaches unprecedented levels, sea level rise is accelerating, northern forests and tundra are releasing more carbon dioxide than they absorb, the Greenland ice sheet has lost about 129 gigatons of ice (or roughly 129 billion metric tons), and other major ecological systems like tropical coral reefs , the Amazon rainforest , and Antarctica’s ice sheet are being pushed toward catastrophic tipping points.

While Trump campaigns for eight Nobel Peace Prizes, his war on humanity’s only home continues unabated, a slow-motion destruction that threatens us all. My parents couldn’t have imagined a leader in the White House who would put McCarthy to shame and push the country — and the world — to the precipice of doom: a commander-in-chief worthy of the name President Apocalypse.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
